doc.title: Mandel Johnny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Childhood, schooling and the New York band scene
title: Hotel rooms, theaters and the corny bands
summary: He describes hearing bands at the Park Central, the New Yorker, the Astor and the stage shows, including Sammy Kaye and Guy Lombardo.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: I heard him at the Park Central, I heard Larry Clinton at the Park Central I remember at the time. Park Central which is now the Omni Park in New York, it was a, has a room, or probably still for all I know it’s still there, it was up on the top.
Oh you mean, that room doesn’t get used for anything I imagine.

It had a great bandstand and good sounding room. Lotta bands, bands played there all the times in the 20s, I think Ben Pollack was there with Benny Goodman and the band, Jack Teagarden. It was, it was a real good band spot. And we’d go to the New Yorker and hear bands, I heard Benny Goodman there, heard Tommy Dorsey up at the Astor Roof later. You know there were just a, and I’d go hear them at all the stage shows, the Paramount changed every few weeks, the Strand changed every two weeks, every few weeks. I’d go catch every damn show. I used to run around New York all by myself in those days, even, when you’re a kid it was easy then.

Totally safe and there was the [inaudible] state even then I realized was the graveyard of bands, but I went and you know, so you’d hear the 2nd rate and 3rd rate bands and you’d hear some people that were… I went to every damn place I could find, whenever, wherever there was

a band, even the bad, I even went and saw some of the Mickey Mouse bands, like Sammy Kaye and those, and you know when you’re that young, you don’t censor that much. I drew the line at Guy Lombardo though.

I didn’t realize until later on that he was a marvelous replica of a mid-20s dance band. That had never changed his style and to me it just sounded corny and weird and out of tune and everything but hearing it now, it wasn’t atypical of what went on in the 20s at all.
The whole thing, tuba was your bass; you know you had the tuba, you had the two pianos, you had like… it was a whole different feel. Banjo on the off beats and then later guitar.
And he stayed with the tuba.
And him waving his baton out of time.
